title: Classification and Exact Local Masking in Finite-Field Clifford Dual-Unitary Circuits
abstract: We classify two-qudit finite-field Clifford dual-unitary gates and apply the classification to exact local masking and operator transport in homogeneous brickwork circuits. Under ordered one-qudit Clifford equivalence, the dual-unitary locus contains $q-2$ perfect-tensor cores, one rank-one core, and one SWAP core. The perfect cores are indexed by \[ δ=\det B=\det C, \] and are related to the ordered cross-ratio $λ$ of the associated $[4,2,3]_q$ MDS configuration through \[ λ=\fracδ{δ-1}. \] Homogeneous repetition separates these cores into five transport phases whose algebraic codimensions in $\operatorname{Sp}(4,q)$ are $0,1,2,3,4$.   The one-site Weyl edge channels determine exact local-masking distances. Perfect-tensor circuits attain \[ d_1(t)=4t, \qquad d_2(t)=4t-2, \] whereas delayed erasers satisfy \[ d_1(t)=4t-2, \qquad d_2(t)=4t-4 \] for $t\geq 2$. Consequently, sufficiently short quantum messages are completely hidden from every one- or two-qudit output subsystem, even when the input is entangled with a reference, while remaining exactly recoverable from the full output.   For $q=3$, we construct an explicit perfect-tensor Clifford gate from two inverse SUM gates. Exhaustive Weyl-support searches for $t=1,2,3$ reproduce the predicted masking distances, and a one-period Choi-channel calculation for a four-qutrit periodic circuit gives numerical residual leakage below $2\times 10^{-16}$. Under the coherent perturbation considered here, local leakage is linear in the perturbation strength, whereas the infidelity of recovery using the ideal inverse is quadratic near the perfect point.
summary: This theoretical work classifies complex two-qudit Clifford circuits over finite fields and derives precise formulas for local masking distances. It proves that short quantum messages can be perfectly hidden from partial output measurements while remaining fully recoverable from the whole system. This advances the understanding of information security in quantum computation architectures.
main_problem: The paper classifies two-qudit finite-field Clifford dual-unitary gates and applies this classification to determine exact local masking and operator transport properties in homogeneous brickwork circuits.
main_result: It establishes specific, quantifiable masking laws ($d_1(t), d_2(t)$) showing that short quantum messages can be perfectly hidden from small output subsystems while remaining fully recoverable from the total output.
method: The analysis uses algebraic techniques involving symplectic groups $	ext{Sp}(4, q)$, classifying gates based on determinants ($\delta$) and relating them to geometric structures like MDS configurations and cross-ratios.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by Clifford dual-unitary circuits operating over finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$ on qudits. The dynamics are analyzed using symplectic matrix representations within the group $	ext{Sp}(4, q)$.
key_observables: Local masking distances ($d_1(t), d_2(t)$), entanglement entropy profiles, and algebraic codimensions of transport phases.
important_parameters: The finite field size $q$, the circuit depth $t$, and the determinant parameter $\delta$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes specific structures for homogeneous repetition and focuses on exact local masking (state-independent reduction), distinguishing it from approximate indistinguishability.
figures_summary: Figures/tables summarize phase counts, leakage vs. perturbation strength ($\epsilon$), and recovery fidelity versus Pauli noise probability ($p$).
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by classifying the dual-unitary locus into $q$ core types (perfect, rank-one, SWAP), then analyzing how homogeneous repetition separates these cores into five distinct transport phases with varying algebraic codimensions. Finally, it derives explicit masking laws and tests them numerically for small $q$.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework connecting finite field algebra ($	ext{Sp}(4, q)$) to fundamental quantum information tasks like perfect data hiding provides deep insights into the structure of quantum gates.
